blocks.text: Network topology refers to the layout of a computer network. It explains how devices and cables are arranged. Topology can be physical or logical. Physical topology shows actual connections. Logical topology shows how data flows in the network. Topology affects network performance and maintenance.

In bus topology, all devices are connected to a single main cable. Data travels along this cable to reach each devices. It is simple and low in cost. Failure of the main cable can stop the entire network (as shown in Figure 1.8). It is suitable for small networks. Bus topology is not good for large networks.

blocks.alt: Bus topology: six devices (two desktop computers, a laptop, two servers and a printer) each joined by a short cable to one long main cable; each end of the main cable has a terminator, labelled Terminator.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.8: Bus Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.8).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 1.8 breaks the main cable in the middle and hangs two of the six devices only on a thin line between devices. In a bus topology every device connects to one continuous main cable, as drawn above.

In star topology, all devices connect to a central hub or switch (as shown in Figure 1.9). Data passes through the central device. It is easy to manage and expand. Failure of one device does not affect others. Failure of the central hub stops the network. Star topology is widely used in modern networks.

blocks.alt: Star topology: a desktop computer, a mobile phone, a laptop and a printer each joined by a dashed link, with an arrow, to one central hub or switch.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.9: Star Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.9).

blocks.text: In ring topology, devices are connected in a circular path (as shown in Figure 1.10). Data moves in one direction around the ring. Each device receives data and passes it along. Failure of one device can affect the whole network. It is more complex than bus topology. Ring topology is rarely used today.

blocks.alt: Ring topology: devices placed on one circular cable: two tower computers, two desktop computers, a laptop, a printer and a globe with a Wi-Fi sign at the top.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.10: Ring Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.10).

blocks.title: Class Activity
blocks.text: Students stand in a circle and pass a message. Discuss what happens if one student stops.

In mesh topology, devices are connected to many other devices. Multiple paths exist for data transmission. This increases reliability and fault tolerance. Failure of one link does not stop communication. Mesh topology is expensive and complex. It is used in large and critical networks.

Figure 1.11 shows a mesh topology network. In this topology, each device is connected to many other devices. Data can travel through multiple paths to reach its destination. If one connection fails, data can use another path. This figure explains why mesh topology is very reliable but complex.

blocks.alt: Mesh topology: five devices (a globe with a Wi-Fi sign, two desktop computers, a laptop and a printer), each joined by a separate line to every other device.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.11: Mesh Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.11).

blocks.text: In tree topology, devices are arranged in a hierarchical structure like a tree (as shown in Figure 1.12). It combines features of both bus and star topologies, where multiple star networks are connected to a central backbone. Data flows from the root (main node) to branches and sub-branches. It is easy to expand and manage large networks. However, failure of the backbone can affect the entire network. Tree topology is commonly used in large organizations.

blocks.alt: Tree topology: a vertical Backbone Cable with end caps. Concentrator (hub) S1 joins nodes A, B and C; concentrator S2 joins nodes D, E and F; a third concentrator (hub), fed from S2, joins nodes G, H and I. A server is joined directly to the backbone. Labels: Nodes, S1, S2, Concentrator (Hub), Server, Backbone Cable.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.12: Tree Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.12).

blocks.text: Advantages and Disadvantages of Network Topologies

Different topologies offer different benefits. Some are easy to install and low-cost (as shown in Table 1.1). Others provide high reliability and performance. Certain topologies are easy to expand. Some are difficult to manage and expensive. Choosing the right topology depends on network needs.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Some topologies are simple and cheap. Others are reliable but costly. Some are easy to expand. Others are difficult to manage. Choice depends on needs.
